Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How difficult is it to change research field after getting a PhD?
Answer: It can be very difficult, and was basically impossible for me. It depends on the types of “transferable skills” (I hate that term) you develop along the course of a PhD. Some PhDs, such as physics, EE, and economics, may help develop strong math and programming skills, which can be used in other areas. Other disciplines (such as organic chemistry)… not so much. The skills involved in being able to do an asymmetric addition of an alkylzinc to an aldehyde are not really useful in other areas.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: What did you learn "the hard way"?
Answer: Getting a job after a degree (B.S., PhD, whatever) is not about what you know, it’s about who you know. These days, having a degree is not considered a major accomplishment like it was in our parents’ generation. Degree holders of any kind are dime a dozen nowadays, and so in order to get your foot in the door and get a interview/job at any company you need connections and someone who can vouch for your skills.

Question: Do you regret getting your Ph.D.? Why or why not?
Answer: A little, because it has closed off a lot of career paths and opportunities, and has not really helped with getting any new ones. I’m yet to get any mileage or benefit out of it. The tragic thing is that I’m still underqualified (or unqualified) for jobs in my field due to the global oversaturation of PhD’s in chemistry.

Name: Arjun Narayanan
Question: How has your PhD helped your career, and do you recommend it?
Answer: My PhD has not helped my career, and I wouldn’t recommend it. It is much, much, much more difficult to find a job and get your career started with a Ph.D. (as compared to a Master’s or Bachelor’s). The current oversupply of college graduates is beginning to spill over into other areas as well - a lot of these graduates are also pursuing advanced degrees (e.g. MBAs, Ph.D.s, or other degrees) in order to distinguish themselves, leading to a glut of graduates with these advanced degrees as well. In the sciences (e.g. chemistry and biology), this is especially bad. Due to the way graduate education is set up in the United States, we have a well-documented glut of Ph.D. scientists and not enough academic or industrial positions to take them all in. In terms of career advancement and progress, getting a Ph.D. has been a net negative so far, for me. However - if you love research, if you love your subject, and if you love the idea of delving deeply into it and becoming a world master in a small niche in it (that nobody may know about or care about), then by all means go for it. Just be aware that the payoff at the end of the road is nonexistent (or even negative).
